core: The working definition of life insurance, anchored to NAIC: a contract in which the policyholder pays premiums and the insurer pays a benefit to named beneficiaries when the insured person dies
Why life insurance exists: income replacement for dependents, with an original example (a parent whose salary supports the household)
The four core terms with one line each, anchored to the NAIC consumer glossary: policyholder, beneficiary, death benefit, premium

Term versus whole: term covers a set period (commonly 10, 20, or 30 years) with no savings component and typically lower premiums; whole covers the entire life with a cash-value component and typically higher premiums
The general, non-advisory logic of coverage amounts: the benefit exists to replace income and settle debts, so the amount relates to those needs (no specific amounts, no buying advice)
Who typically needs life insurance: people whose dependents rely on their income — a factual general pattern, not a recommendation
The honest framing: life insurance is about the people left behind — the insured never receives the benefit; the named beneficiaries do
supporting: The premium keeps the policy in force; coverage ends if premiums lapse or, for term, if the term expires before death
The policyholder and the beneficiary can be different people — the payer and the receiver are separate roles
Federal money guidance (MyMoney.gov Protect) frames insurance as part of protecting yourself against life's unexpected events
outOfScope: Specific coverage amounts, policy shopping, and buying recommendations (NO FINANCIAL ADVICE rule)
Riders, underwriting, medical exams, and other policy-detail mechanics
Annuities, investment uses of life insurance, and estate-planning strategies
Tax treatment of death benefits and jurisdiction-specific insurance law
Health insurance depth (own sibling topic: personal-finance:foundations:health-insurance-basics) and general insurance mechanics (own sibling topic: personal-finance:foundations:insurance)

claims.claim: Life insurance is a contract: the policyholder pays premiums, and when the insured person dies, the insurer pays a benefit to the named beneficiaries.
The purpose of life insurance is income replacement for dependents: the benefit supports the people who relied on the insured's income after the insured dies.
Term life insurance provides coverage for a set period — commonly 10, 20, or 30 years — has no savings component, and typically carries a lower premium than whole life.
Whole life insurance provides coverage for the insured's entire life and includes a cash-value (savings-like) component, and typically carries a higher premium than term.

The NAIC consumer glossary defines the four roles and amounts that carry a life insurance contract: the policyholder owns the policy and pays the premiums, the beneficiary is named to receive the death benefit, the death benefit is the amount paid to the beneficiaries when the insured dies, and the premium is the payment that keeps the policy in force.

Who typically needs life insurance follows a general factual pattern: people whose dependents rely on their income are the ones whose death would cost others the most, which is why income replacement is the classic reason to hold life insurance.

Coverage amounts follow a general logic rather than a formula: the benefit exists to replace income and settle debts, so the amount is tied to those needs; specific amounts are a personal decision and are not stated in the lesson.
Federal money guidance (MyMoney.gov) frames insurance as part of the Protect principle: protecting yourself against life's unexpected events includes insurance.
The honest framing of life insurance: it is about the people left behind — the insured never receives the benefit; the named beneficiaries do, and only while the policy is active.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is whole life insurance a savings product?
positions: NAIC: whole life covers the insured's entire life and includes a cash-value component, which can look like saving inside a policy.
NAIC: term life has no savings component at all and typically costs less — the products differ in both coverage period and price.
The lesson's honest frame: life insurance is protection for the people left behind; the cash value is a feature of one product type, not the point of life insurance generally.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents term and whole factually side by side (coverage period, savings component, typical premium level) and keeps the framing that life insurance is protection, not a savings plan. No product is declared universally better.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much life insurance should someone buy?
positions: General logic: the amount should relate to the needs the benefit must cover — replacing income and settling debts.
Specific dollar amounts vary with each household's income, expenses, and debts and are a personal decision.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the general needs-based logic and explicitly gives no specific amounts or buying advice, consistent with the project's no-financial-advice rule.
